title: Pool covers: handling, storage and the limits of a cover
audience: Pool service technicians who handle, check and store pool covers on home pools
learningOutcomes: Identify heat-retaining, winter debris and power-operated covers and what each is for
Explain why no cover is a complete safety control and what other measures the owner must consider
Handle, roll, clean and store a cover so that it is not damaged and does not become a hazard
Record the state of the cover and any referral needed for a lockable or power-operated cover

instruction.heading: Cover types
instruction.body: Heat-retaining covers rest on the surface, cut evaporation and the heat lost to cold wind, and need no fixings. Bubble covers are a common heat-retaining type. Winter debris covers are stretched across the pool, keep leaves and blossom out, and are fixed to the surround. Power-operated covers can be locked and come in fabric or slatted plastic. The UK handbook notes that floating covers keep much debris out, but debris can drop back in when the cover is lifted. Identify the cover type before you handle it.

instruction.heading: A cover is not a complete safety control
instruction.body: The UK handbook is direct that no swimming pool cover is a complete safety control. A safety cover only protects when it is laid over the pool while nobody is using it, and only when it is checked and kept in working order. A winter debris cover, even one in sound condition and firmly anchored, must not be relied on for any level of safety. In some cases fencing or other measures are needed, and that is judged case by case. Supervision still applies whenever the pool is open, as “Supervision, behaviour rules and drowning prevention at home pools” explains. Record what you see, and never describe a cover as a barrier or certify it.

instruction.heading: Handling and rolling
instruction.body: Use a suitable roller to make a cover easier to manage. A cover should not be left rolled or folded, and never left in strong sunlight in that state, because the material can be damaged. Lift a floating cover slowly so debris sitting on it does not drop back into the water gradually a cover left on the pool during icy weather deteriorates, so take it off or inspect it during cold spells.

instruction.heading: Cleaning and storage
instruction.body: Before storage, clear away all debris and wash the cover. Avoid solvents, because they make the material shrink. Store it somewhere sheltered, away from heat and concentrated chemicals. Keep a winter debris cover above the waterline where possible. A heavy snow load can press the cover down onto the water, which then carries the weight. If a cover has frozen in place, leave it alone, because forcing it will damage the material.

instruction.heading: Power-operated and lockable covers
instruction.body: A lockable cover only protects when it is locked. At each visit, check the lock, the drive, the controls and the cover edges, and record any fault. The drive is electrical equipment, so any wiring or drive repair goes to a licensed electrician. Do not run a power cover that shows a visible fault, or that has anyone in its path.

procedure: Identify the cover type and record it on the visit form.
Check the cover, the lock, the fixings and the straps for damage, and record the state.
Remove debris from the cover before lifting it, and lift it carefully to keep debris from the water.
Roll the cover on a suitable roller and do not leave it rolled or folded in strong sunlight.
Clean the cover using water and a suitable cleaner, not with solvents, and let it dry.
Store the cover in a sheltered place, away from heat and concentrated chemicals.
For a power cover, test the lock and controls only if the owner has asked you to, and refer any fault to a licensed electrician.
Record the cover type, its state, the action taken and any referral.

workedExamples.situation: The owner asks you to describe their cover as 'safe for the children' on the service note because it has a lock.
workedExamples.reasoning: Write what you observed: the cover type, its state, and that the lock was or was not engaged. Do not describe the cover as safe for children. The handbook says no cover is a complete safety control. Add the advice that supervision continues whenever the pool is open.

workedExamples.situation: A floating heat-retaining cover is wrinkled on one side and is sitting in strong sunlight, rolled loosely on the pool edge.
workedExamples.reasoning: Lift the cover carefully so that debris does not fall in. Clean it without solvents, lay it flat in shade or roll it properly on a roller. Record the wrinkling and the sunlight exposure, and advise the owner to store the cover correctly. Do not leave the cover rolled or folded in the sun.

equipmentAndPpe: Cleaning brush and water; no solvents
Non-slip footwear for the pool surround
Record sheet for cover type and condition

commonErrors.error: Describing a cover as the complete safety control
commonErrors.prevention: Record the cover as one layer and keep supervision advice in writing.

commonErrors.error: Cleaning a cover with a solvent
commonErrors.prevention: Use water and a suitable cleaner only. Solvents shrink the material.

commonErrors.error: Leaving a cover rolled, folded or in strong sun
commonErrors.prevention: Roll it on a roller and store it in shade.

commonErrors.error: Lifting a floating cover so that debris falls back to the water
commonErrors.prevention: Remove debris first and lift the cover carefully.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: No swimming pool cover is a complete safety control. Where a cover is used, further measures like fencing may be needed, and the decision is case by case.
A safety cover must be placed over the pool once it is unused by bathers, and it must be lockable where it is designed to lock.
Do not leave a cover rolled, folded or left open to strong sunlight.
Do not clean a cover with solvents, because they cause shrinkage.
A winter debris cover must not be taken to be to give any level of safety, even when it is kept in good order and firmly anchored.
Wiring, drive and controls of power-operated covers are electrical work. Refer them to a licensed electrician.

qualityStandard: Cover type, condition and lock state are recorded at each visit.
No cover is described as a complete safety control.
The cover is cleaned without solvents and stored correctly, with the storage recorded.
documentationEvidence: Cover type, condition, lock state and action record
Referral note for power-operated cover faults
Written advice to the owner on the limits of a cover
summary: A cover reduces heat loss and debris but is never a complete safety control.
Roll, clean and store covers so they are not damaged or left in the sun.
Refer any power or lock fault to a licensed person.

knowledgeChecks.question: A homeowner says their pool cover makes the pool safe for children. What is the correct response?
options: Remove the cover so that the children can see the water and then let them wade in at the shallow end
Tell the owner that a winter debris cover forms a full barrier and that the children are safe in it
Agree and record whether the pool is complete safe and sign the record for the owner each week
Explain that no cover is a complete safety control, and that supervision and other measures still apply

knowledgeChecks.question: A floating cover has been left rolled in strong sunlight. What is the correct action?
options: Remove debris, clean without solvents, roll it correctly and store it in shade
Leave it, since the sun will dry it and it will be fine by tomorrow
Clean it with a solvent to remove the debris and dry it in the sun
Fold it tightly so it fits under the pool edge and leave it in the sun

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must a cover be cleaned without solvents?
options: Solvents make it heavier to lift
Solvents cause the cover to shrink
Solvents are not allowed near water
